data.title: Signing judgments and orders
sentences: (1) A judge or applications judge may sign a judgment or order when it is pronounced.
(2) If a judge or applications judge does not sign a judgment or order when it is pronounced, the court clerk may sign the judgment or order in any of the following circumstances:
(a) in a proceeding which a party adverse in interest did not attend
(b) if the party adverse in interest approves the form of the judgment or order or waives approval of its form
(c) if the Court directs that approval of the form of the judgment or order by a party is not required
(d) if the Court directs the court clerk to sign the judgment or order.

(3) In any circumstance other than those described in subrule (2), a judgment or order must be signed by a judge or applications judge. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.4 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)
Alta.* Reg. 136/2022, s. 1(8) effective September 1, 2022 (Alta. Gaz. June 30, 2022)]

commentary.text:
This rule permits signature of an order by the applications judge or judge when it is pronounced, or by the court clerk in certain circumstances where the order is not signed at pronouncement. There is also the practice, where an order is not signed on pronouncement, for the parties to submit the order later to the judge or applications judge who granted it when the order has been agreed as to form and signed by counsel to the parties.
Pursuant to rule 9.4(2), the court clerk may sign the judgment or order where the requirements of that rule are met.
Rule 9.4(2)(c) is discretionary and is often invoked in foreclosure proceedings. Beazer v. Tollestrup Estate, [2017] A.J. No. 1380, 2017 ABCA 430 at para. 80 (Alta. C.A.). Further, it is also invoked where there is a self-represented party involved and the court sees fit to dispense with the self-represented party approving and signing the form of order, as would otherwise be required under rule 9.2(2)(b). When rule 9.4(2)(c) is invoked, the court is implicitly relying on counsel for the represented party acting as an officer of the court and pursuant to professional ethics to accurately and fairly prepare the form of order.
Costs Against Counsel – When counsel prepares an order incorrectly and then makes subsequent submissions relying on their own drafting error, the court may award costs against legal counsel personally. Svenderus v. Engi, [2019] A.J. No. 517, 2019 ABCA 155 at paras. 17-20 (Alta. C.A.).

data.title: Effective date of judgments and orders
data.text:
Every judgment and every order, whether or not it has been entered, comes into effect on (a) the date of pronouncement, or (b) if the Court orders the judgment or order to come into effect before or after the date of pronouncement, the date so ordered.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.6 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

(a) the date of pronouncement, or

(b) if the Court orders the judgment or order to come into effect before or after the date of pronouncement, the date so ordered. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.6 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text: The presumption is that judgments and orders are effective from the date of pronouncement, which means the parties must act pursuant to such orders and judgments prior to the order being signed and entered, unless otherwise ordered by the court.

data.title: Certified copies
data.text:
(1) On entry of a judgment or order, the court clerk must, without additional charge, certify a copy of it for the party who enters the judgment or order.
(2) A certified copy of a judgment or order has the same effect as the original.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.7 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

data.title: Service of judgments and orders
data.text:
Unless these rules otherwise provide or the Court otherwise orders, the party who enters the judgment or order must serve a copy of the entered judgment or order on each of the other parties.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.8 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

hierarchy.heading: Division 2 – DETERMINATION OF DAMAGES, JUDGMENT IN COUNTERCLAIMS AND JUDGMENT AGAINST BENEFICIARIES

rules.title: Determining damages
rules.text:
The Court must determine damages for a continuing claim to the time the Court makes its determination of the amount.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.9 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*
sentences: The Court must determine damages for a continuing claim to the time the Court makes its determination of the amount. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.9 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text: Pursuant to this rule, damages are calculated up to the time of determination. The interpretation of rule 9.9 is not restricted to damages claims. The quantification of a liquidated claim is almost by definition always far simpler than a damage claim and is also permitted under this rule. Condominium Corp. No. 0825873 v. 1246153 Alberta Ltd., [2011] A.J. No. 309, 2011 ABQB 178 at para. 7 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).

rules.title: Judgment for balance on counterclaim
rules.text:
The Court may give judgment for the balance of money to be paid by one party to the other when determining a counterclaim.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.10 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

rules.title: Judgment against beneficiaries
rules.text:
A personal representative or trustee entitled to a judgment or order for the administration of an estate or the execution of a trust may have the judgment or order made against any person beneficially interested in the estate or trust.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.11 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

info_notes: If a party dies before judgment but after all evidence is heard, rule 4.35 [Death has no effect on an action after evidence heard] applies.

rules.title: Correcting mistakes or errors
rules.text:
On application, the Court may correct a mistake or error in a judgment or order arising from an accident, slip or omission.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.12 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

rules.title: Re-opening case
rules.text: At any time before a judgment or order is entered, the Court may (a) vary the judgment or order, or (b) on application, and if the Court is satisfied there is good reason to do so, hear more evidence and change or modify its judgment or order R. 9.13 [Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.13 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]

rules.title: Further or other order after judgment or order entered
rules.text:
On applica- tion, the Court may, after a judgment or order has been entered, make any further or other order that is required, if (a) doing so does not require the original judgment or order to be varied, and (b) the further or other order is needed to provide a remedy to which a party is entitled in connection with the judgment or order.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.14 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*
sentences: On applica- tion, the Court may, after a judgment or order has been entered, make any further or other order that is required, if
(a) doing so does not require the original judgment or order to be varied, and

(b) the further or other order is needed to provide a remedy to which a party is entitled in connection with the judgment or order. *[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.14 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*
info_notes: If an application is made under this rule, note that rule 6.3(1) [Applications generally] provides for an application to be made after judgment.

commentary.text:
Rule 9.14 empowers a court to make a further order when that is needed in order to provide the litigants with the relief to which they are entitled under the original order. Strathcona (County) v. Hansen, [2014] A.J. No. 19, 2014 ABCA 17 at para. 6 (Alta. C.A.). Typically it is used to “give effect to the judge’s original intention”. Ting v. Ting Yassa v. Parker , [2024] A.J. No. 42, 2024 ABKB 25 at para. 36 (Alta. K.B.); , [2018] A.J. No. 485, 2018 ABQB 305 at para. 31 (Alta. Q.B.) and , 2022 ABKB 818 at G. (A.A.) v. G. (J.L.) paras. 20-23 (Alta. K.B.).
However, rule 9.14 cannot support an application to reconsider and vary a judgment previously pronounced. AGF Trust Co. v. Mcleod, [2011] A.J. No. 1257, 2011 ABQB 711 at para. 13 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)). The common thread among rules altering judgments “is the Court’s discretion”. The nature of the change requested, and the status of the order or judgment are both factors that are considered. Howland v. Chekowski, [2013] A.J. No. 688, 2013 ABQB 364 at para. 9 (Alta. Q.B.).
Rule 9.14 grants a judge jurisdiction, after an order has been perfected, to make any further or other orders that are required to provide a remedy to which a party is entitled the original order. The judge has the ability to grant these further vis a vis orders, but only if the further orders would not result in a variation of the original order. If the requirements of rule 9.14 are met, the court may issue further orders whether the original order is interlocutory or final. First Calgary Financial Credit Union Ltd. v. Inspired Luxury Homes Inc., [2014] A.J. No. 1467, Rule 9.14 “does not preclude a Judge from clarifying, supplementing or working out the terms of her Order, but in any event, no legislation, including the Rules, should be read to limit a superior court judge’s ability to maintain supervision over the enforcement of their Exception to the Rule Functus – Rule 9.14 “is a narrow exception from the normal rule that [ ], once it has made a final functus offıcio decision”. Richter v. Chemerinski, [2014] A.J. No. 566, 2014 ABQB 322 at para. 4 (Alta. Q.B.).

rules.title: Setting aside, varying and discharging judgments and orders
rules.text:
(1) On application, the Court may set aside, vary or discharge a judgment or an order, whether final or interlocutory, that was made (a) without notice to one or more affected persons, or (b) following a trial or hearing at which an affected person did not appear because of an accident or mistake or because of insufficient notice of the trial or hearing.
(2) Unless the Court otherwise orders, the application must be made within Westpoint Capital Corp. v. Solomon Spruce Ridge Inc., [2017] A.J. No. 1462, 2017 ABQB 497 at para. 9 (Alta. Q.B.). days after the earlier of (a) the service of the judgment or order on the applicant, and (b) the date the judgment or order first came to the applicant’s attention.
(3) The Court may, on any terms the Court considers just, (a) permit a defence to be filed by a party who has been noted in default, (b) set aside, vary or discharge a judgment granted upon application against a defendant who was noted in default, or whose statement of defence was struck out under rule 3.37, or (c) set aside, vary or discharge a judgment entered in default of defence by the plaintiff for the recovery of property under rule 3.38, or for a debt or liquidated demand under rule 3.39.
(4) The Court may set aside, vary or discharge an interlocutory order (a) because information arose or was discovered after the order was made, (b) with the agreement of every party, or (c) on other grounds that the Court considers just.

rules.title: Enforcement: orders for payment and judgments for payment into Court
rules.text:
(1) An order for payment may be enforced in any manner in which a judgment for the payment of money may be enforced.
(2) A judgment for the payment of money into Court may be enforced in any manner in which a judgment for the payment of money to a person may be enforced.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.17 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

rules.title: Judgments and orders subject to conditions
rules.text:
(1) If a judgment or order is made subject to conditions that a party must fulfil, a party to whom the conditions apply may not do anything further to enforce the judgment or order until (a) the party has filed an affidavit confirming that the conditions have been met, or (b) the Court so permits.
(2) An application to do anything further may be filed without notice to any other party unless the Court otherwise orders.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.18 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

rules.title: Persons who are not parties
rules.text:
If a person is not a party to an action but (a) the person obtains an order or an order is obtained in the person’s favour, the person may enforce the order in the same manner as if the person were a party to the action, or (b) the person is subject to a judgment or order granted in respect of that action, the judgment or order may be enforced against the person in the same manner as if the person were a party to the action.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.19 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

This rule makes it clear that non-parties to an action can both enforce the benefit of, and bear the burden of, certain orders and judgments.
Rule 9.19(b) would likely only be invoked in the case of non-monetary orders or judgments. It is a departure from the basic rule of (“listen to the other audi alteram partem side”). Mella99in the context of a fraudulent conveyance where the transferee has not been made a party.

rules.text:
Unless an enactment otherwise provides, and except for the purpose of the enactment, a writ remains in force as long as the judgment or order under which the writ was issued is in force.

rules.title: Application for new judgment or order
rules.text:
(1) On application, the Court may grant a judgment creditor a new judgment or order on a former judgment or any part of it that has not been paid.
(2) Repealed AR 128/2015 s7.
(3) Notice of the application must (a) be filed before the expiry of the limitation period under the Limitations Act for an action on the judgment, and (b) be served on the judgment debtor by the same method by which a commencement document must be served.
(4) An application under this rule is an application in the original action.
(5) If the judgment debtor does not appear at the hearing of the application, and show cause why a new judgment or order should be denied, the Court may grant the judgment creditor a new judgment or order for the amount due and a costs award if the Court is satisfied that (a) notice of the application was served on the judgment debtor, and (b) the amount has not been paid under the original judgment or order.
(6) If the judgment debtor opposes the judgment creditor’s application in whole or in part, the Court may (a) give directions for the trial of an issue, and (b) make any procedural order the Court considers necessary.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.21 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010); Alta.*

rules.title: Application that judgment or order has been satisfied
rules.text:
(1) On application, the Court may make an order that a judgment or order has been satisfied.
(2) The application must (a) be in Form 41, (b) be filed, and (c) be served on the affected parties by the same method by which a commencement document must be served.
(3) The court clerk must include in the court file a memorandum that a judgment or order has been satisfied if (a) the Court so orders, or (b) the judgment creditor or the judgment creditor’s lawyer acknowl- edges in writing that the judgment or order has been satisfied.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.22 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text: Sometimes a plaintiff (judgment creditor) cannot be found. Where the amount owing is clear, applications judges frequently direct that the amount of the judgment be paid to the clerk of the court and upon such payment being made, the judgment is then deemed satisfied. This application is not, technically, an application under rule 9.22, but it invokes the analogy rule (rule 1.7(2) and takes into account paragraph 9.22(2)(c)). The applications judge normally then directs substitutional service of the order by the best approach available, as would be done for substitutional service of a statement of claim or originating application.

rules.title: Order of possession of land
rules.text:
(1) This rule applies when a judgment or order of possession orders a person to give up possession of land to another person.
(2) A judgment or order of possession must include a statement to the effect that a civil enforcement agency has authority, after service of the order has been effected, to evict any occupant of the land.
(3) Unless the Court otherwise orders, the judgment or order of possession must be served on every person ordered to give up possession of the land and every occupant of the land.

rules.text:
(1) A person who enforces a judgment or order of possession in respect of premises need not remove personal property from the premises.
(2) If a civil enforcement agency removes and stores any personal property in connection with the enforcement of a judgment or order of possession, the owner of the personal property may, on the written authorization of the civil enforcement agency, obtain the personal property from storage by (a) paying to the civil enforcement agency the costs, including trans- portation and storage costs, that were paid by the civil enforcement agency or by the person on whose behalf the judgment or order of possession was enforced, and (b) paying to the person storing the personal property any further outstanding storage charges.
(3) If personal property is sold in accordance with an order made under an enactment, the proceeds of sale must be applied as follows:
(a) first, to pay the costs of the sale;
(b) second, to pay storage, transportation and other costs incurred in removing and storing the personal property and filing the applica- tion for the order for sale;
(c) third, unless the Court otherwise orders or an enactment otherwise provides, to pay the balance to the owner of the personal property.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 9.27 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

rules.title: Abandoned goods
rules.text:
(1) In this rule, (a) “abandoned goods” means personal property left on land or at premises by a person who has (i) been evicted from the land or premises by a civil enforcement agency, or (ii) vacated the land or premises as a result of a judgment or order of possession;
(b) “judgment holder” means a person who has a judgment or order of possession.
PART  Condominium Corp. No. 0825873 v. 1246153 Alberta Ltd., [2011] A.J. No. 309, 2011 ABQB 178 at para. 7 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).
(2) A judgment holder may dispose of abandoned goods if the judgment holder believes on reasonable grounds that the abandoned goods have a market value of less than $2000.
(3) Even though abandoned goods have a market value of $2000 or more, a judgment holder may sell the goods by a means and for a price that the judgment holder believes is reasonable if the judgment holder believes on reasonable grounds that (a) storing the abandoned goods would be unsanitary or unsafe or would rapidly result in total or substantial depreciation of the market value of the goods, or (b) the cost of removing, storing and selling the goods would exceed the proceeds of their sale.
(4) If subrules (2) and (3) do not apply, the judgment holder (a) must store or arrange for storage of the abandoned goods on behalf of the owner or person entitled to possession for one month after the date of their abandonment, and (b) after the one month has expired, may dispose of the goods by public auction or, with the approval of the Court, by private sale.
(5) If no bid is received for the abandoned goods at a public auction held under subrule (4)(b), the judgment holder may dispose of the goods.
(6) No liability attaches to a person for (a) selling abandoned goods under subrule (3) or (4)(b), or (b) disposing of abandoned goods under subrule (2) or (5).
(7) If abandoned goods are disposed of or sold under this rule, the person acquiring the goods on the disposal or sale acquires the interest of the owner or person entitled to possess those goods, and the interest of any other person in those goods is extinguished.
(8) A judgment holder must give up possession of abandoned goods to the person entitled to them on payment of the costs of removing and storing them.
(9) A judgment holder (a) may apply the proceeds of any sale of abandoned goods (i) to the judgment holder’s costs of removing, storing and selling the goods, and (ii) to satisfy the judgment debtor’s liability to the judgment holder, and (b) must pay the surplus of the proceeds of sale after payment under clause (a), if any, to the Crown in right of Alberta.
(10) The President of Treasury Board and Minister of Finance must retain
